abstracts.abstract: This paper presents a novel game-theoretic framework for modeling adversarial interactions in zero-trust cybersecurity architectures, fundamentally departing from traditional perimeter-based security models. Unlike conventional approaches that assume static trust boundaries, our framework treats network security as a continuous Bayesian game between defenders deploying microsegmentation strategies and sophisticated adversaries conducting multi-stage attacks. We formulate the interaction as a dynamic Stackelberg game with incomplete information, where defender strategies include continuous authentication, least-privilege access control, and behavioral analytics deployment. Our theoretical analysis yields several significant contributions: First, we prove the existence of a sequential equilibrium that characterizes optimal defender resource allocation under uncertain threat intelligence. Second, we derive closed-form expressions for threshold-based detection policies that minimize expected damage from advanced persistent threats. Third, we demonstrate that the proposed framework naturally captures the kill-chain progression inherent in modern cyberattacks. The game-theoretic analysis reveals counterintuitive insights regarding the optimal balance between preventive controls and detection mechanisms. This work establishes a rigorous mathematical foundation for zero-trust architecture design, providing verifiable security guarantees that traditional heuristic-based approaches cannot offer. Our framework addresses fundamental challenges in cybersecurity economics and adversarial risk management, opening new theoretical directions for adaptive security policy synthesis.

This paper provides a comprehensive security analysis of lattice-based cryptographic constructions under the lens of quantum algebraic attacks, offering substantial theoretical improvements over existing reductionist security proofs. While current NIST post-quantum standards rely on hardness assumptions regarding lattice problems, we identify critical gaps in their security models when facing hybrid attack strategies combining classical and quantum computational paradigms. Our analysis introduces a refined framework for evaluating Ring-Learning-with-Errors (RLWE) security that accounts for quantum speedups in solving shortest vector problems through a combination of Grover's algorithm and quantum walk techniques. We establish tighter bounds on the quantum attack complexity for key encapsulation mechanisms, demonstrating that previous security estimates may be overly optimistic by factors ranging from 2^15 to 2^30 for practical parameter sets. The theoretical contributions include: a novel reduction from module-LWE to decision-LWE that preserves quantum security properties; an improved模 analysis of NTRU Prime under quantum adversaries; and concrete parameter recommendations for achieving 256-bit quantum security. Furthermore, we prove that certain algebraic manipulations previously considered quantum-secure exhibit structural vulnerabilities when subjected to our enhanced attack model. These findings have direct implications for the design of next-generation cryptographic protocols in data security applications.

We introduce DeepMesh, a distributed intrusion detection system designed for next-generation edge computing infrastructures that fundamentally reimagines threat detection through federated learning and edge-native processing. Traditional centralized security analytics architectures introduce prohibitive latency and privacy concerns in distributed environments. DeepMesh addresses these challenges by deploying lightweight neural network models across edge nodes, enabling real-time detection of sophisticated attacks without transmitting sensitive network traffic to centralized analysis platforms. The system architecture comprises three novel components: an adaptive feature extraction layer that dynamically selects network flow characteristics based on traffic volatility; a consensus-based model aggregation protocol that preserves differential privacy while achieving detection accuracy comparable to centralized approaches; and a hierarchical alert correlation engine that synthesizes distributed detection signals into coherent threat narratives. Our implementation demonstrates that DeepMesh achieves 98.7% detection accuracy for novel attack vectors including zero-day exploits and polymorphic malware, with inference latency under 5 milliseconds at the network edge. The federated learning framework enables continuous model improvement without compromising data sovereignty, addressing critical compliance requirements in regulated industries. Security analytics show a 73% reduction in false positive rates compared to signature-based systems while maintaining resilience against model poisoning attacks. This work establishes a new architectural paradigm for cyber threat intelligence in distributed computing environments.

This paper presents SmartAnalyzer, an enhanced malware analysis platform that significantly advances automated static and dynamic analysis capabilities for modern ransomware and advanced persistent threats. Existing sandboxes suffer from critical limitations including evasion susceptibility, limited symbolic execution coverage, and inadequate handling of anti-analysis techniques prevalent in contemporary malware. SmartAnalyzer addresses these deficiencies through three architectural innovations: a hardware-assisted virtualization layer that defeats environment detection by exposing authentic hardware states to guest samples; a hybrid symbolic execution engine combining static binary lifting with dynamic concolic testing to achieve comprehensive code coverage; and a graph neural network-based behavioral classification module that identifies malicious code families with 96.4% accuracy. The system implements novel techniques for reconstructing encrypted network communications and extracting command-and-control infrastructure details that existing tools frequently miss. Evaluation against a corpus of 50,000 malware samples demonstrates substantial improvements: 89% reduction in evasion successes, 340% increase in code coverage for heavily obfuscated samples, and extraction of 41% more indicators of compromise compared to leading commercial sandboxes. SmartAnalyzer's scalable architecture supports analysis throughput exceeding 1,000 samples per hour while maintaining precise malware family attribution. The platform provides security operations centers with actionable threat intelligence, enabling rapid response to emerging campaigns through automated indicator extraction and yara rule generation.
